---
abstract: "*All children with Down syndrome experience delays acquiring language skills. By describing trajectories of vocabulary development we can offer families and practitioners insights into expected ranges and rates of progress. These can help to inform teaching goals and methods, and to identify children experiencing more complex or challenging difficulties. This study pools data from multiple sources to provide estimates of trajectories of word learning and distributions of expected spoken, signed and understood word counts at 6-monthly intervals for children with Down syndrome aged 12 months to 6 years.*"

# Introduction {#sec-intro}

Children with Down syndrome experience difficulties learning language [@naessLanguageVerbalShortterm2011; @abbedutoLanguageDevelopmentSyndrome2020] and this adversely impacts many aspects of their lives. They learn the meanings of words and learn to say words more slowly than most other children [@naessDifferencesSimilaritiesPredictors2021]. Learning vocabulary is a foundational skill: it is important for learning broader language skills, including grammar, and for learning to read [@naessReadingSkillsChildren2012; @hulmeGrowthReadingSkills2012].

## Practical importance

Understanding vocabulary development matters for practice because teaching and therapy are most effective when they are matched to what a child currently knows and can do. An accurate description of typical trajectories identifies how a child's vocabulary compares with that of other children at the same age. It can also indicate what usually comes next -- what children with this vocabulary are typically ready to learn. Vocabulary is well suited to guiding practice in this way because it is observable and countable in ways that many other language skills are not. Parents can observe and record the words their child understands, says and signs [@hutchinsMacArthurBatesCommunicative2013; @deckersConcurrentPredictiveValidity2016; @millerValidityParentReport1995], and progress is visible word by word as new words are learned.

The progress a child has made in their vocabulary development can inform what they can learn next across language, speech and reading. Words are a prerequisite for learning grammar. Vocabulary size therefore indicates readiness to move from teaching first words to teaching two-word phrases and, later, sentence structures [@fensonVariabilityEarlyCommunicative1994; @batesInseparabilityGrammarLexicon1997; @zampiniLexicalSyntacticDevelopment2011; @sepulvedaCanIndividualsSyndrome2013]. Children practise saying the words they know and attempt. A child's productive vocabulary therefore defines the opportunities available for practising speech sounds and improving clarity. When learning to read, children most readily learn to read words that are already in their vocabulary, and vocabulary knowledge predicts later reading development and comprehension [@naessReadingSkillsChildren2012; @hulmeGrowthReadingSkills2012]. Reading instruction can, in turn, offer a further route for teaching new vocabulary and supporting spoken language. Knowing where a child is on each of these fronts helps parents and practitioners to choose teaching targets that are neither so far ahead of the child that they result in frustration, nor so far behind that they fail to move learning forward.

## Existing research

The development of language skills among children with Down syndrome has been the subject of many research studies over many decades. Yet, there remains a lack of broadly applicable practical data to guide families and practitioners. Existing data sets are generally small. A recent review of studies of vocabulary among children with a variety of developmental conditions reported 17 studies of children with Down syndrome with sample sizes ranging from 6 to 40 and a median sample size of 25 [@laudanskaCommunicativeDevelopmentInventories2026]. Individually, these studies are insufficient for providing reliable estimates of typical vocabulary development (@sec-large-dataset).

Parents, practitioners and people with Down syndrome have recently called for researchers to make it easier to access evidence-based information of practical relevance to real-life issues, suggesting past research has not focused enough on issues that might make meaningful differences to their lives [@cristescuShapeResearchChange2024]. In our experience, families and educators are interested in information about vocabulary development in children with Down syndrome, including the range of words understood or spoken at different ages, rates of word learning, and the range of ages at which a minimum number of words may be learned.

## Study aims

This study therefore aims to describe the development of vocabulary knowledge in children with Down syndrome with a focus on interpretable statistics that can inform teaching and support. Specifically, we aim to:

- Characterise trajectories of word learning and spoken and signed production among children with Down syndrome aged 12 months to 6 years
- Estimate the ranges of words understood, signed or spoken by children with Down syndrome at 6-monthly intervals from 12 to 72 months
- Identify the proportions of children with Down syndrome reaching specific vocabulary milestones at different ages
- Contrast vocabulary development among children with Down syndrome with that of typically developing children

## A large dataset {#sec-large-dataset}

Accurate estimates of trends in vocabulary development over time and distributions of words learned at particular ages require many observations of many children.

The precision of an estimated average improves only with the square root of the number of observations [@gelmanRegressionOtherStories2020, chapter 16; @wainerMostDangerousEquation2007]. Therefore, halving uncertainty requires four times the data. Estimates from small samples also differ from each other more than estimates from large samples do -- that is, they are more prone to sampling error [@bergmannPromotingReplicabilityDevelopmental2018; @schubertImprovingStatisticalReporting2025]. For example, if the spread between children at a given age has standard deviation $\sigma$, the average estimated from $n$ children typically misses the truth by $\sigma/\sqrt{n}$. Therefore, two studies of 20 children each will typically report averages about a third of the whole between-child spread apart ($\sqrt{2}\,\sigma/\sqrt{n}$) through chance alone, before any real difference between their populations, settings or measures is counted. 

Sample sizes matter even more for characterising trajectories. A trajectory incorporates many estimates. Average word counts at each age are estimated from nearby observations. Consequently, the data are divided among the ages they describe. Moreover, the quantities of most practical value are ranges rather than averages. These are properties of the spread between children, estimated from differences among children. Spreads require more data than an average does and statements about the edges of a range depend on the children observed least often.

The consequences are clearly visible in published estimates of vocabulary at around 36 months. Even the largest study to date, with 330 children, observed only 31 of them at age 3;0, reporting a median spoken vocabulary of 16 words and a mean of 36 [@berglundParentalReportsSpoken2001]. Smaller studies report means of about 48 words (from 18 children observed at 36 months) [@zampiniVocabularyDevelopmentChildren2013] and 54 words (from 10 children reaching two-word phrases at a mean age of 37 months) [@oliverLanguageDevelopmentChildren1994]. Differences in locations, languages, instruments, in how children were recruited and in whether a mean or a median is reported account for part of this spread -- but with samples of these sizes, no single study can distinguish its own sampling variation from real differences, nor say much about the range between children that is of most practical interest.

Therefore, to maximise the precision of our estimates we pool parent observations of vocabulary learning in 846 children with Down syndrome from 14 datasets collected by charities and research groups in 6 countries (@sec-data). For comparisons, we pool parent reports of words learned by children without identified difficulties ('typically developing') from 18 datasets in 6 countries (~37,700 children).

## Statistical modelling and Bayesian inference

To identify trajectories and to estimate expected ranges of word learning, we develop statistical models that describe how children's vocabulary grows over time and how it varies between individuals (@sec-models). We fit these models using Bayesian inference [@gelmanRegressionOtherStories2020; @mcelreathStatisticalRethinkingBayesian2020].

Bayesian analysis treats probability as a measure of uncertainty about unknown quantities [@gillBayesianSocialScience2024]. Estimates derived from Bayesian inference take the form of probability distributions and support direct statements such as: "given our model and the data, there is an 89% probability that a 36-month-old child with Down syndrome understands up to 142 words." [**TODO**: update example with final estimate] Traditional (frequentist) statistical methods do not license statements of this kind: a confidence interval describes how the estimating procedure behaves across repeated samples, not the probability that the true value lies within it [@moreyFallacyPlacingConfidence2016]. For a study that aims to give families and practitioners usable expectations, probability statements that mean what most readers take them to mean offer a clear advantage [@wagenmakersBayesianInferencePsychology2018; @mcelreathStatisticalRethinkingBayesian2020].

Bayesian inference also provides a principled way to use existing knowledge of vocabulary development, through prior distributions ("priors"). Priors are assumptions that are stated explicitly, evaluated, and tested for sensitivity like every other part of a model [@gelmanBayesianWorkflow2020; @gelmanStatisticalWorkflow2026; @mcelreathStatisticalRethinkingBayesian2020]. Bayesian inference also supports direct predictions for unobserved children, which is precisely what setting expectations for an individual child requires.

## Summary

This study aims to provide practical information about vocabulary development among children with Down syndrome that is of use to families, practitioners and researchers. To do so, we pool parent-reported vocabulary observations from multiple studies of children with Down syndrome and fit Bayesian models to them. This methodology is intended to provide reliable estimates of trajectories and expected ranges of words understood, spoken and signed that can inform support, early intervention and teaching approaches.
